text: I’ll model the fluid passage itself: lower centreline from \((0,0)\) to \((120,0)\) mm, a right-hand semicircle centred at \((120,15)\) mm with 15 mm centreline radius, then the upper leg back to \((0,30)\) mm. The 10 mm width gives bend radii of 10 and 20 mm. I’ll use a structured, one-cell-thick 3D extrusion with `empty` front/back patches, which is the standard OpenFOAM representation of a planar 2D incompressible domain. First I’m constructing and plotting the coarse CAD fluid volume.

The coarse shape is correct and the four requested dimensions match. I’ll now write a structured `blockMesh` topology: 60 cells along each straight, 24 through the bend, 5 across the passage, and 1 through the assumed 1 mm thickness (720 hexahedra total). Curved `arc` edges preserve the 10/20 mm bend radii rather than polygonalizing the walls.

The topology is written as 14 connected blocks with explicit inlet, outlet, wall, and `empty` front/back face groups. I’ll generate the coarse mesh now and inspect `blockMesh`’s topology report before refining or exporting surfaces.

`blockMesh` did not start because an empty case has no `controlDict`; no mesh was modified. I’ll add the minimal OpenFOAM case metadata needed by mesh utilities, without adding solver settings or boundary conditions.
The required case metadata is now present. I’ll rerun `blockMesh` and review its face matching and cell creation report.

The mesher succeeded interactively, but that cell was not replay-safe because its `subprocess` import came from the earlier failed cell. I’ll repeat it with an explicit import so the final `build.py` reproduces the mesh from an empty directory.

The coarse mesh has 720 hexahedra and the intended patch counts. I’ll now look at the actual structured grid in plan view, including every cell edge; this is the coarse visual check before deciding whether the mesh needs refinement.

The coarse mesh conforms cleanly, but five cells across a 10 mm passage is only a geometry-validation mesh. For a more useful incompressible-flow starting mesh, I’ll uniformly refine by four in both planar directions: 20 cells across the duct, 0.5 mm cells in the straight legs, and about 0.49 mm centreline spacing through the bend. This remains modest at 11,520 cells.
The final resolution is now encoded. I’ll regenerate the mesh and verify the final cell and patch counts before running the binding quality check.

The final mesh contains 11,520 cells with 20 inlet and outlet faces, 1,152 wall faces, and two complete `empty` planes. Before quality checking, I’ll inspect the available OpenFOAM surface exporter so the named mesh patches can also be delivered as separate STL files without re-selecting them geometrically.

`foamToSurface` exports the combined boundary and does not expose per-patch selection in its short options. I’ll check the patch-selective `surfaceMeshExtract` interface instead, so each STL inherits its OpenFOAM patch name directly.

`surfaceMeshExtract` supports exact patch-name selection. I’ll export `inlet`, `outlet`, `walls`, and `frontAndBack` separately from the final mesh; this preserves the patch assignment made in `blockMeshDict` and avoids any coordinate-based relabeling.

The extractor correctly wrote the three non-empty boundary patches, but OpenFOAM intentionally omitted the `empty` patch (the 27-byte file contains no facets). I’ll explicitly tessellate the two computational planes from the same structured coordinates, with outward \(-z\) and \(+z\) winding. This supplies the complete named surface set while retaining `empty` behavior in the mesh.

All four named surface files now contain facets, and together represent the closed extruded fluid volume. I’ll run `checkMesh -allGeometry -allTopology`; this is the binding validation for cell topology, openness, non-orthogonality, skewness, and determinant quality.

`checkMesh` stopped immediately after reading the mesh, before reporting any geometry metric; the diagnostic was on stderr and was not printed by that failed cell. I’ll rerun it only to expose the complete error message, without changing the mesh.

The mesh itself was not rejected; `-allGeometry` requires an `fvSchemes` dictionary even for a mesh-only case. I’ll add a minimal standard incompressible finite-volume schemes file solely so the extended geometry checks can execute; no fields or boundary conditions are being created.
The extended-check dependency is now present. I’ll rerun the complete topology and geometry validation and save its output in `checkMesh.log`.

The extended mode also requires `fvSolution` to exist, again before checking any cells. I’ll add an empty mesh-only dictionary; it contains no solver configuration and merely satisfies the utility’s case parser.
Both parser dependencies are now available. I’ll rerun the extended `checkMesh` validation.

`checkMesh` passes all checks, but its volume exposed a CAD bookkeeping issue: the mesh volume is \(2.87115\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^3}\), while the first CAD solid reported less because `Box` uses centred default alignment in-plane. The structured mesh coordinates are correct, but the delivered STEP must match them. I’ll rebuild the CAD with explicit minimum alignment for the straight and clipping boxes, then verify its bounds and analytical volume before re-exporting.

The mesh is valid, but the advisory STL-union check found 768 free edges and coplanar crossings. This is not acceptable to waive: the hand-generated front/back triangulation did not reproduce `blockMesh`’s curved-edge interpolation exactly. I’ll inspect the native `polyMesh` file format and regenerate every STL patch from the same point and face arrays, guaranteeing shared coordinates and winding.

The native mesh is ASCII and provides exact boundary face ranges. I’ll now replace all four STL files by triangulating those exact outward-oriented OpenFOAM faces. Every patch interface will therefore share bit-identical vertices, including the curved bend.

The parser accidentally treated the `FoamFile` header dictionary as a boundary patch. I’ll filter dictionary blocks to those containing both `nFaces` and `startFace`, then repeat the exact-mesh export in a replay-safe cell.

All STL patches now come directly from the validated mesh: 24,232 boundary faces triangulated with exact shared points and native outward winding. This fixes the prior curved-edge mismatch rather than waiving it. The geometry, STEP, structured mesh, patch surfaces, and successful `checkMesh.log` are complete.
